item.title: Activity-based temporal hypergraphs: from individual activity to collective social dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.36333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal hypergraphs provide an interesting representation for many social systems, as they integrate both the temporal and group nature of social interactions. Designing models of time-varying hyper-networks yields thus a convenient way to generate surrogates of empirical social systems, to understand the mechanisms underlying their emergent properties, and to investigate the evolution of dynamical processes taking place on such structures. Here, we focus on a specific and powerful class of these models, the activity-based temporal hypergraphs. We show how activity mechanisms provide control over the time scale of the dynamics, allow high modelling flexibility, and capture heterogeneity in agents' behavior. We also highlight how the activity can straightforwardly be extracted from empirical data to create surrogate datasets. We present paradigmatic examples of such models: the higher-order activity-driven models (HADx), which show that different underlying rules for the selection of active interactions produce different higher-order dynamics; the Emerging Activity Temporal Hypergraph model (EATH), able to generate surrogates of empirical systems by using higher-order mechanisms driven by both activity and group memory. We conclude discussing future perspectives for activity-based temporal hypergraphs, highlighting the potential of this framework to bridge realistic modelling of social dynamics with the study of the complex dynamical process they can support, from social contagion to opinion dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Marco Mancastroppa, Giulia Cencetti, Iacopo Iacopini, Giovanni Petri, Alain Barrat

item.title: Feedback autocratic strategies in stochastic games
item.description: arXiv:2610.36683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A stochastic game is an optimal control problem for multiple agents in a stochastic environment. Stochastic games contain important practical problems, related to environmental issues or traffic flows. If the number of environmental states is one, such stochastic games are called repeated games. In repeated games, several strategies which unilaterally control payoffs have been proposed, and these strategies work in a mechanism similar to feedback control. In this paper, we generalize these strategies as feedback strategies in stochastic games, and investigate their properties. In particular, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for such feedback strategies to work as controllers of payoffs under some assumptions. We demonstrate the performance of such feedback strategies in several examples related to social dilemmas. Our findings connect the theory of payoff control in repeated games to the theory of feedback control in stochastic games.
item.dc:creator: Masahiko Ueda

item.title: Superlinear cities, finite limits: Three characteristic scales of urban agglomeration
item.description: arXiv:2610.37029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Urban scaling research has established that many socioeconomic outputs increase superlinearly with city population, implying rising per-capita output. Although urban scaling models have incorporated infrastructural and dissipative costs, they have generally not identified the finite population scales implied by independently scaling benefits and diseconomies. We connect the classical urban-economic trade-off between agglomeration benefits and costs to a generalized scaling framework in which these quantities follow distinct power laws. When diseconomies scale more rapidly than benefits the model yields three ordered characteristic populations: the first (smallest) maximizes net benefit per capita; the second maximizes total net benefit; and the third (largest), at which aggregate benefits equal diseconomies. Their absolute values depend on the magnitudes of benefits and costs, but their relative separation depends only on the scaling exponents. We illustrate these relationships using published scaling estimates from several countries, and examine aggregate and extensive--intensive scaling across 102 Australian Significant Urban Areas. Aggregate employee income, rental payments and daily journey to work commuting distances for journeys scale superlinearly, although the aggregate rent--income exponent difference is statistically inconclusive. Mean rent per reporting renter household and estimated mean distance for daily commutes increase more rapidly with city population than mean employee income per earner. These findings reveal intensive differences obscured by aggregate scaling. The framework shows how superlinear agglomeration benefits can coexist with still faster-scaling diseconomies and produce finite characteristic urban scales without requiring benefits themselves to become sublinear.
item.dc:creator: Somwrita Sarkar

item.title: Mapping Artistic Engagement with Quantum Technologies
item.description: arXiv:2610.37054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum technologies (QT) are increasingly being taken up in artistic practices, for example in the form of visual artworks or quantum computer music. However, more comprehensive empirical studies on the temporal development and the different forms of QT-related art are still lacking. Therefore, this study conducted a systematic mapping and classification of QT-related artworks. To this end, a medium-independent corpus was established, and the artworks were classified into four categories: QT-Inspired, QT-Sourced, Simulated QT, and QT-Generated. This classification was LLM-assisted and checked against human-coded reference data as well as through manual review of unclear cases. In total, 281 QT-related artworks from 2010 to August 2025 were identified. The corpus shows a substantial increase in QT-related artworks since 2019, with a considerable share attributed to only a few artists. The different forms of QT relations coexist, while an increasing use of active hardware-based and simulated processes in artistic practices can be documented, particularly since 2021. Although no clear development trajectories between these categories can be identified, the observed development coincides with advances in QT and their improved accessibility. Thus, this study provides an empirical basis for further analyzing the development of QT-related art, the possible emergence of a "quantum art scene," and the reciprocal relationships between art and quantum technologies.
item.dc:creator: Adrian Schmidt, Oya Ok, Deniz \.Ipek Zeynio\u{g}lu, Zeki C. Seskir

item.title: Beyond urban boundaries: Percolation reveals land-consumptive growth in India
item.description: arXiv:2610.37073v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cities often extend beyond their administrative boundaries, complicating assessments of urban sustainability. Using Global Human Settlement Layer data for India's 50 largest urban agglomerations (1975--2025), we develop a percolation-based framework for urban delineation. Within district-based regions, we apply unrestricted DBSCAN to spatial coordinates of 100-m cells with positive population and built-up surface. We treat neighborhood distance as the percolation control parameter and the proportion of eligible cells in the largest connected cluster as the empirical order parameter. Sharp increases in this proportion reveal characteristic percolation transitions. Post-transition connection lengths declined (median:650m to 350m), indicating that previously disconnected settlements coalesce at progressively shorter spatial distances alongside increasing urban land consumption. Urban footprint increased from 447.6 to 1,382.7km$^2$, while population densities declined. SDG11.3.1 land-consumption-to-population-growth ratios generally exceeded unity. Zipf and allometric relationships describe cross-sectional urban structure, but land-consumptive growth shows little relationship with city size. Urban delineation thus shapes sustainability assessments.
item.dc:creator: Somwrita Sarkar, Chirag Deb, Carolina Pantoja Mardones, Anmol Gaur, Arunim Anand, Rashi Shrivastava, Anusha Roy, Arnab Jana, Eswar Rajasekaran, David Levinson

item.title: Detailed balance and phase transition in Nash equilibria of mean-field Ising game
item.description: arXiv:2610.36518v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a finite-state mean-field game with entropic control cost. In the large population limit, we show that its stationary Nash equilibria satisfy the detailed balance condition and their distributions take the Gibbsian form with the value function playing the role of a Hamiltonian. We apply the entropic control cost to a ferromagnetic mean-field Ising game and investigate its stationary and non-stationary Nash equilibria. We find that the stationary Nash equilibria exhibit a second-order phase transition from disordered to ordered equilibria as temperature decreases. A center-manifold reduction yields non-stationary Nash equilibrium near the critical temperature and reveals the critical slowing down in the relaxation toward the stationary Nash equilibrium.
item.dc:creator: Ken Hiura, Hajime Koike, Kiyoshi Kanazawa

item.title: Neighborhood Deprivation Shapes Post-Flood Population Losses in Pune and Bandung
item.description: arXiv:2610.37418v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Disaster research in high-income settings shows that better-resourced communities see population inflows and faster recovery, while disadvantaged communities suffer prolonged population loss. Whether this pattern holds in rapidly urbanizing cities of the Global South remains unclear. Here we show, using mobile phone data from Pune, India, and Bandung, Indonesia, how neighborhood-level changes in phone presence, a proxy for short-term population movement, relate to flooding and neighborhood deprivation. We combine satellite-derived flood maps with phone records to compare flooded and non-flooded areas over the 30 days around each flood. In both cities, less deprived neighborhoods see phone presence rise after flooding, while more deprived neighborhoods see it fall, consistent with resource-seeking interpretations documented in North American and European disaster research. The cities differed, however, in how deprivation relates to flood exposure: in Pune, more deprived flooded neighborhoods showed suggestive evidence of disproportionately larger decreases in detected device presence than similarly deprived non-flooded neighborhoods; no comparable interaction was observed in Bandung. Economic considerations are associated with post-flood device-presence changes in South and Southeast Asian cities in ways that parallel high-income contexts, though local context adds variation.
item.dc:creator: Sukie Xiuqi Yang, Guangyuan Weng, Shiyue Cui, Zhicong Chen, Catherine Chen

item.title: Urban scaling and the dynamics of individual cities
item.description: arXiv:2603.30021v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cities are often compared through scaling laws, usually expressed as power-law relations between population size and aggregate urban quantities related to infrastructure, socioeconomic activity, or environmental impacts. These laws are influential because their exponent is often interpreted as describing what happens when a city grows, with implications for urban theory, planning, and policy. Here, we show that this interpretation is generally misleading. An exponent measured by comparing many cities at one date does not, in general, describe the trajectory of any individual city. Instead, it reflects a statistical pattern produced by cities with different histories, constraints, institutions, and growth paths. Apparent sublinear or superlinear scaling can therefore arise even when individual cities follow simpler dynamics, as we show for the area--population relation. Cross-sectional scaling laws can reveal system-level regularities, but should not be used alone to infer growth mechanisms or guide policy for a given city.
item.dc:creator: Ulysse Marquis, Marc Barthelemy

item.title: A method for including additional socio-demographic factors in social contact matrices for compartment-based epidemic models
item.description: arXiv:2605.13870v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Socio-demographic factors influence social contact patterns and play a fundamental role in shaping the transmission dynamics of infectious diseases. However, compartment-based models of infectious disease dynamics commonly consider the dependence of contact patterns on age, but ignore other factors that are likely to have compounding effects. Methods that stratify the population by multiple socio-demographic factors are few and require social contact surveys that contain information about all factors of interest. Here we present a method that can stratify an existing social contact matrix with an additional socio-demographic factor using information about the population structure of the socio-demographic factors and assumptions about the aggregate mixing rates within and between groups. We then analyse hypothetical populations and a projection of a social contact survey onto Aotearoa New Zealand's age-ethnic structure to show how these extended social contact matrices can change epidemic dynamics and outcomes. The inclusion of the additional factor has a big impact on the model reproduction number and final epidemic size. We find that minority group epidemic outcomes are most sensitive to variation in model parameter values.
item.dc:creator: Vincent X. Lomas, Tim Chambers, Leighton Watson, Michael Plank

item.title: Enabling quantum communication in ultra-large-scale networks
item.description: arXiv:2606.08326v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The recent development of small-scale quantum networks poses the question of which network-level mechanisms could enable quantum communication to operate at scale in a future Quantum Internet. The question can be answered within a well-established framework where a quantum network is mapped into a classical weighted graph, and communication reliability is assessed using methods from network theory. Previous work relied on this framework to determine sufficient conditions for viable network-wide communication only on special network topologies, such as regular lattices, and to devise communication protocols applicable only to small- and moderate-sized real networks. Here, we overcome both limitations by introducing a family of quantum communication protocols that scale to networks with hundreds of millions of nodes. We show that the competition between increasing communication distance and path redundancy determines their large-scale behavior, and that degree heterogeneity can provide sufficient redundancy to sustain communication in small-world networks. These conclusions are supported by a systematic analysis of both real network topologies and synthetic networks, and an analytical treatment in the limit of infinitely large random scale-free graphs.
item.dc:creator: Filippo Radicchi

item.title: Tracking High-Impact Researchers Through Highly Cited Tails
item.description: arXiv:2610.11891v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: It is well recognised that field weighted citations are approximately lognormally distributed. This skewness reflects competition for attention, whereby most publications are gradually forgotten and only a minority continue to be recalled years later. Exploiting this observation, we construct a researcher-level indicator based on authorship of top 10% cited papers in All Science Journal Code (ASJC) bins and apply it to publications affiliated with Irish institutions over a typical funding cycle. Restricting attention largely to original research papers, we find that researchers authoring strictly more than one ASJC top-decile paper in a given year exhibit persistent participation in the highly cited tail of the literature in subsequent years, thus the simple track record indicator possesses predictive value. In contrast, the median researcher in cohorts of Research Ireland and European Research Council awardees selected through qualitative peer review either authors no top-decile paper or less than the median researcher in our ranking. These results demonstrate that research excellence as judged by qualitative peer review and influence on the research literature identify substantially different cohorts of researchers. In the absence of evidence, funding bodies and universities may conflate these two. While research reputation may be enhanced through many channels, highly cited papers constitute the most widely observable manifestation of international scholarly influence. Our analysis indicates that literature influence may be improved through greater use of data in track record pre-screening prior to qualitative peer review.
item.dc:creator: Hirushan Sajindra, Eoin \'O Colg\'ain
